title: Sublime Draw
reviewNotes: Reconstructed the initial pawn sacrifices and opposition timing. This is a verified drawing study, with deliberately losing Kb2 compared against the drawing Kb1. Practice goal is hold the draw.
transcript: Fools will resign because it seems clear that the black king [music] is fast enough to pick up the white pawns. If you try to run to defend them, now actually black is going to push us back and there is going [music] to be no way to avoid the loss of the pawns. So, black is just going to win this position. And of course, if instead we try to push the pawn, we're always going to lose it either like this or like this. So, should white resign? Well, not exactly because in this position white does have an incredible [music] way to draw the game. And it all starts with the brilliant idea B6. A surprising concept. Didn't we say that we cannot push or we're just going to lose the pawn? Well, you see, first of all, if the king takes, now we have gained one precious tempo to get closer with our king and maintain the pawn. So, this would be a draw. But of course, black is under no obligation of capturing that pawn with the king. It can simply be captured by the black pawn. And now again, if you try to get closer to the pawn, black is just going to keep us away and then pick it up and we still lose the game. Seems impossible to draw this position with white. And yet it isn't because white can sacrifice the other pawn, too. Pawn to C5. If black allows us to take, there is going to be no pawn for him to push. But of course, he can still capture this pawn. And now we end up in an end game where black is the only one with a pawn. But it is important to understand that a king and pawn end game can be drawn under the perfect conditions. It all depends on who has the opposition. For example, if we now push the king to B2, black is going to be playing king to B4. And now black gains the opposition on the king. Meaning that actually over time, he's going to push the king to the side and start pushing the pawn. And there is no way for us to stop it. So, white needs to be the one gaining the opposition, which means that [music] paradoxically, the only move that holds this game is king to b1. A move that seems very counterintuitive, staying away from the action, but this is the only move that draws because of course, if the black king comes closer, now we are going to be the ones taking the opposition. And actually, this is a textbook drawn endgame. And some of you might think, well, can't black just push the pawn? But no, again, this is another textbook draw. We play king to b2 [music] and it seems like black can gain the opposition. But now, we play king to c2 and the king is blocked by his own pawn. He cannot maintain the opposition, which means that again, this is a drawn position and black is not going to be able to win. [music]
